segment:
They held the contact with each other’s hands, but let their eyes wander around the space. The couch. The fireplace. The window behind them and beyond it the twilight over the bay.
Then Jonah dropped his hand to his side, but leaned in closer so that his shoulder was touching hers, just for a moment. His glasses caught a little glint of light off the lamp behind her.
“Did you have a chance to look around while you were waiting? Your room has a pretty good view.”

“The bay,” Mara agreed, looking toward the water and the lights already coming on across it, “and the highway.”
It was odd being alone with another recruit, since all their communication up to now had been through Adrian’s email. Or she’d been alone, except for those silent meetings in the parking lot when the two of them had had their backgrounds checked.

She saw a man walk in. She glanced at him: mid-twenties, tall, dark, slim.

“Did you arrive this afternoon?” she asked.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

She could tell from his eyes that he was still smiling, though his lips were closed. She dropped her hand but didn’t let herself look away, waiting for his next move.

“Sit down.” He gestured back at the couch with one of his empty hands, and then seemed to realize he had forgotten to introduce himself.

He put both hands together as if he were trying to do it again from scratch.

“I’m Jonah Reed,” he said. “Hardware security and firmware. I came in on Saturday for my residency.”
“I’m Mara Vale, infrastructure security,” she said. “Nice to meet you.”
He grinned again, a little self-deprecatingly this time. “Well, that’s a start.”

“Can I help?” she asked.

“You’re a guest,” he said. “Why don’t you take a seat? Let me get us some drinks.”
And he turned to the bar and poured himself a beer without waiting for her reply.

segment:
He broke the awkwardness.
“I’m sorry if I startled you. I was expecting someone else, and—I guess—I was a little nervous myself.”
He didn’t let go of her hand just yet, so she couldn’t see his face without turning sideways. She felt herself smiling as she gave a short laugh, and then realized he had just been making a joke at his own expense.
“How long have you worked here?”
“I’ve only been here for two days,” he said. “But Adrian told me about you when we were at lunch today.”
He finally let go of her hand so that she could look him in the eye again, and smiled his big boy-next-door smile.
She had never seen anyone who could pull off glasses like those before; they didn’t look stupid or nerdy but rather somehow serious, intelligent even. He wasn’t wearing any other kind of jewelry besides an ordinary wristwatch; it didn’t seem to have anything to do with his style at all.
